title: is that a hat?
hook: what's under the turban, what the color means, and the plain steel circle on the wrist

segments.voice: Yesterday: langar, where nobody sits higher. Today, the questions a lot of Sikhs get asked at school and at work.

Is that a hat? What's under there? Does the color mean something? Sikhs who wear a turban hear these at school, at work and in the airport security line. The real answers are better than most people expect. And there's a second thing that often needs explaining, on the wrist: a plain steel circle.
screen: `IS THAT A HAT?` → `WHAT'S UNDER THERE?` → `AND THE CIRCLE ON THE WRIST.`

segments.voice: Start underneath. Many Sikhs keep their hair uncut all their lives, as a way of accepting the body as it was made. That's kesh. The turban, the dastar or pagg, covers and looks after that hair. So no, it isn't a hat that comes off with the weather. Most who wear one tie it fresh each morning, over hair combed and knotted on top, yards of cloth wrapped layer by layer. It's a skill: first tries come out lopsided for everyone, and practice does the rest. Sikh tradition remembers that in the Gurus' world a fine turban marked kings and nobles. The tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, made it part of his community's identity, so every Sikh who ties one wears a crown, whatever family they come from. The color? For most, simply a choice, or what goes with the day. And not every Sikh wears one: some women do, many cover their hair with a scarf, and Sikhs keep the faith in different ways. If you've cut your hair, you're every bit as welcome on this path. Now the wrist. The kara is a plain steel bracelet: a circle with no beginning and no end, like the one God. Steel, not gold, on purpose. It isn't jewelry. Sikhs often say that when your hand reaches for something, the kara gets there first and asks: should my hand be doing this?
screen: `KESH — HAIR, LEFT AS IT GREW.` · `THE DASTAR — A CROWN YOU TIE.` · `THE COLOR IS USUALLY A CHOICE.` · `THE KARA — STEEL, NOT GOLD.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, sit up and let the crown of your head rise, as if something precious rested there. On the second, touch your wrist, where a kara would sit. On the third, think of one thing your hands will reach for today.
The turban. A crown tied fresh over hair left as it grew, and beside it, the steel kara. Third word.
Your line: a crown you tie yourself. Next time someone asks if it's a hat, that's the short answer. Day three.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs keep their hair uncut; men and some women tie a turban fresh each day, others cover their hair with a scarf, and many Sikhs, including some who don't keep the other articles of faith, wear a steel kara on the wrist. Everyone covers their head in the gurdwara.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: dastar, a respectful word for the turban; it comes from Persian.

trapdoor: what you thought: a religious hat.
what it means: a crown tied over uncut hair, and on the wrist a steel circle that reminds the hand before it acts.

what a scholar hears: dastar is a Persian loanword, and in the Gurus' era turbans marked rank, so a whole community wearing them was a statement of equal dignity. kesh and kara are two of the five Ks the Khalsa keeps.

story.title: two gold bracelets
story.text: A wealthy follower once brought Guru Gobind Singh a pair of gold bracelets set with jewels, the finest he could find. The Guru, sitting by a river, turned one over in his hands and tossed it into the water. The man dove in and searched until he came up empty. Where exactly did it fall? he asked. The Guru threw the second one in. Right there.
story.source: a popular sakhi of Guru Gobind Singh, told in several versions

wrong.myth: the turban is a hat, and its color shows a group.
wrong.truth: it's a crown tied over uncut hair, and for most Sikhs the color is simply a choice.

notes: Sensitive topic: the script says not every Sikh wears a turban and 'Sikhs keep the faith in different ways' without taking a side. Keepers may want different wording (the Rehat Maryada requires kesh for amritdhari Sikhs; research: don't treat non-kesdhari Sikhs as less).
